one_line: Walkthrough of FOKS, an open-source, federated, Go-based alternative to Keybase for end-to-end encrypted git and key-value secrets, with post-quantum hybrid encryption and a short setup demo.
summary: The video introduces FOKS (Federated Open Key Service; captions render it as "Fox"), an open-source Keybase-style tool written in Go for end-to-end encrypted git repos and key-value storage, aimed at API keys, configs and sensitive files. The speaker's main claims are that clients, not the server, hold the keys, so a server breach exposes only ciphertext, and that users can pick or self-host a federated server to avoid vendor lock-in. The demo runs the setup on the default fox.app federated server: start the control agent, sign up with an email, username and device name, list keys, create a remote repo, then clone it, which turns on encryption automatically. Pushed files reach the server as ciphertext, and keys can be revoked by ID. For post-quantum security the speaker says FOKS layers Curve25519 with the ML-KEM algorithm, so an attacker would need to break both, though he admits he does not fully understand ML-KEM. The product is in beta, and the speaker says mobile apps, sync-based file systems and encrypted chat are planned. The video offers no benchmarks, threat model or independent audit, so the security claims are the vendor's.

key_ideas.idea: Client-held keys are the core security claim
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says the client, not the server, controls the keys, so a hacked server yields only ciphertext. This is a vendor claim; the video shows no threat model or audit.

key_ideas.idea: Federation is pitched as the answer to vendor lock-in
key_ideas.detail: Users can pick a server whose policies they trust or self-host one. Being open source, the code can be audited, forked or run as a hosting service.

key_ideas.idea: Git contents are encrypted on the client, including file names and history
key_ideas.detail: Commits, file names and history are encrypted locally, so the server stores only ciphertext. The speaker presents this as the main differentiator.

key_ideas.idea: The remote repo is created first, and cloning turns on encryption
key_ideas.detail: fox git create makes the remote repo on the server. Cloning it locally initializes FOKS and enables encryption automatically; after that, normal add, commit and push work and are encrypted transparently.

key_ideas.idea: Key revocation by ID is the recovery story for lost devices
key_ideas.detail: Keys are listed on the server and can be revoked by ID, e.g. after a stolen laptop. The speaker says the other keys then rotate automatically; the video does not show this happening.

key_ideas.idea: Post-quantum protection is a hybrid of Curve25519 and ML-KEM
key_ideas.detail: An attacker would have to break both schemes. The speaker says he does not really understand ML-KEM and is trusting the security experts, so treat this as an unverified summary.

key_ideas.idea: Single-key risk is shown, then waved off for the demo
key_ideas.detail: fox key list warns that losing the only key means losing all access. The demo acknowledges the warning and skips backup-key setup, a step a real deployment needs.
The speaker says FOKS is still beta, with mobile apps, sync-based file systems and encrypted chats planned, and that communities could run their own federated servers.

techniques.name: Set up FOKS and create a user
techniques.how: Install FOKS (the speaker uses Homebrew and says to check the install docs for other platforms). Run `foxctl start` to start the control agent. Run `fox sign up`, press Enter, choose to create a new user, choose a home server (the default is the federated fox.app server, or a custom one), enter an email, optionally an invite code, a username, and a device name for the access key. The captions say `fox` and `foxctl`; the exact binary names should be checked against the docs.
techniques.when: First-time setup on a workstation, or when evaluating FOKS against a self-hosted alternative.

techniques.name: Create an encrypted git repo
techniques.how: Run `fox git create <repo>` to create the remote repo on the server first. Clone it locally. Cloning shows FOKS initializing, which enables encryption for the repo. Then add, commit and push as usual; encryption happens transparently on push.
techniques.when: Storing config files, API keys or sensitive files in git without the server being able to read them.

techniques.name: Inspect and revoke keys
techniques.how: Run `fox key list` to show all keys on the server, then revoke a key by its ID. The speaker says other keys rotate automatically after a revoke; the command names were not clearly captured for this step.
techniques.when: Responding to a lost or stolen device, or auditing which devices hold access.

techniques.name: Acknowledge the single-key warning
techniques.how: When `fox key list` warns that losing the only key means losing access, the demo uses a clear-device-message command to accept the risk. The exact command name is garbled in the captions. In real use, create a backup key first, which the sign-up flow offers.
techniques.when: Only for throwaway demos. Production accounts need a second key or backup first.

numbers.claim: No benchmarks, latency figures, costs, adoption stats or test results are given. The video runs 5:49 and is a setup walkthrough.
Two encryption layers: Curve25519 plus the ML-KEM post-quantum algorithm; an attacker must break both.

hot_takes: Hype title ("Could FOKS Be the FUTURE of Secure Git Hosting?") and "game changer" framing, but the demo is concrete.
The speaker admits he does not understand ML-KEM and relies on trusting security experts, so the post-quantum claim is not checked in the video.
Claims that keys rotate automatically on revoke and that a hacked server reveals nothing are not shown in the demo.
Still beta, and the demo skips backup-key setup, which the video itself flags as the main single-key risk.
Sponsorship: none visible in the transcript.

relevance.why: AgentOS guardrails and the Crucible/exec-gate work touch secrets and credentials for agents. FOKS is a prior-art example of client-held keys and encrypted config storage, but it is not an agent-facing tool.
relevance.action: Read the FOKS white paper and compare its client-held key model with how AgentOS would store provider API keys if that is designed later.

relevance.why: ProsHarness has zero-token credential handling. FOKS's client-held keys and encrypted per-repo config are a related pattern for storing secrets that agent runs need.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness's credential handling against the FOKS key model (client-held keys, revoke by ID, backup key); consider whether it is worth a spike for secret storage.
